chapter_summary:
In Module 3, we explored VLANs as a way to segment a single physical switch into multiple logical broadcast domains. This segmentation is fantastic for security, performance, and management. However, devices in different VLANs, by definition, belong to different IP subnets and cannot communicate with each other directly at Layer 2. This is where **inter-VLAN routing** becomes essential. To allow devices in VLAN 10 (e.g., `192.168.10.0/24`) to communicate with devices in VLAN 20 (e.g., `192.168.20.0/24`), a Layer 3 device, typically a router or a Layer 3 switch, is needed to route packets between these distinct IP subnets. Without inter-VLAN routing, your perfectly segmented VLANs would be isolated islands, defeating the purpose of a connected network.

Modern Arista switches are often capable of performing Layer 3 routing in addition to Layer 2 switching. When a switch performs Layer 3 routing, it's often referred to as a **Layer 3 switch**. The key component that enables a Layer 3 switch to route between VLANs is the **Switched Virtual Interface (SVI)**, also known as a VLAN interface. An SVI is a logical Layer 3 interface associated with a specific VLAN. It acts as the default gateway for all devices within that VLAN. When a device in VLAN 10 wants to communicate with a device in VLAN 20, it sends the packet to its default gateway (the SVI for VLAN 10). The Layer 3 switch then receives the packet on the VLAN 10 SVI, looks up the destination in its routing table, and forwards the packet out the VLAN 20 SVI, which is the gateway for the destination network.

Configuring SVIs on an Arista EOS switch involves a few critical steps. First, you must ensure the VLANs themselves are created and assigned to the appropriate access or trunk ports. Then, you create the SVI for each VLAN by entering `interface Vlan <VLAN_ID>` in configuration mode. Within the SVI interface configuration, you assign an IP address and subnet mask, which will serve as the default gateway for devices in that VLAN. It's crucial that the IP address assigned to the SVI falls within the IP subnet of its corresponding VLAN. Finally, you must enable global IP routing on the switch using the `ip routing` command (and `ipv6 unicast-routing` for IPv6). Without this command, the switch will only perform Layer 2 forwarding, and inter-VLAN routing will not function.

Let's walk through an example of configuring SVIs for VLAN 10 (192.168.10.0/24) and VLAN 20 (192.168.20.0/24) on an Arista switch:

```eos
Arista# configure terminal
Arista(config)# vlan 10
Arista(config-vlan-10)# name Sales
Arista(config-vlan-10)# exit
Arista(config)# vlan 20
Arista(config-vlan-20)# name Marketing
Arista(config-vlan-20)# exit

Arista(config)# ip routing  # Enable global IP routing for IPv4
Arista(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing # Enable global IP routing for IPv6 (if needed)

Arista(config)# interface Vlan 10
Arista(config-if-Vl10)# description Sales_VLAN_SVI
Arista(config-if-Vl10)# ip address 192.168.10.1/24
Arista(config-if-Vl10)# no shutdown
Arista(config-if-Vl10)# exit

Arista(config)# interface Vlan 20
Arista(config-if-Vl20)# description Marketing_VLAN_SVI
Arista(config-if-Vl20)# ip address 192.168.20.1/24
Arista(config-if-Vl20)# no shutdown
Arista(config-if-Vl20)# exit

# Now, assign physical ports to these VLANs (example)
Arista(config)# interface Ethernet 1
Arista(config-if-Et1)# switchport mode access
Arista(config-if-Et1)# switchport access vlan 10
Arista(config-if-Et1)# no shutdown
Arista(config-if-Et1)# exit

Arista(config)# interface Ethernet 2
Arista(config-if-Et2)# switchport mode access
Arista(config-if-Et2)# switchport access vlan 20
Arista(config-if-Et2)# no shutdown
Arista(config-if-Et2)# exit

Arista(config)# end
Arista# show ip interface brief Vlan 10
Arista# show ip interface brief Vlan 20
Arista# show ip route connected
```

After configuring SVIs, verification is key. Use `show ip interface brief Vlan <VLAN_ID>` to confirm the IP address and status of the SVI. `show ip route connected` will show that the networks associated with your SVIs are directly connected. You can also `ping` from the switch to devices in different VLANs or from a device in one VLAN to a device in another VLAN (via its SVI gateway) to test connectivity. Common mistakes include forgetting to enable `ip routing`, assigning an incorrect IP address to the SVI (not matching the VLAN's subnet), or failing to assign physical ports to the respective VLANs. Another common issue is having a shutdown SVI; always ensure `no shutdown` is applied. Safety note: Misconfiguring SVIs can lead to network segmentation breaches or complete loss of connectivity for entire VLANs, so always test changes in a controlled environment first.

However, this segmentation also creates isolated islands, preventing devices in different VLANs from communicating directly. This chapter will show you how to bridge these islands, enabling seamless communication across your segmented network. screens.title: The Necessity of Inter-VLAN Routing
screens.subtitle: Why VLANs Need a Layer 3 Device to Communicate

narration.text: Let's begin by understanding why inter-VLAN routing is so crucial. As you recall from Module 3, VLANs segment a single physical switch into multiple logical broadcast domains. This segmentation is incredibly beneficial for security, performance, and network management. For instance, separating your sales department from your engineering department into different VLANs means their broadcast traffic won't interfere with each other, and you can apply distinct security policies. However, this very segmentation means that devices in different VLANs, by definition, belong to different IP subnets. For example, VLAN 10 might use the 192.168.10.0/24 network, while VLAN 20 uses 192.168.20.0/24. At Layer 2, these devices cannot communicate directly because they are in separate broadcast domains. To allow a device in VLAN 10 to send data to a device in VLAN 20, a Layer 3 device, such as a router or a Layer 3 switch, is absolutely essential. Without this inter-VLAN routing, your perfectly segmented VLANs would remain isolated islands, unable to share resources or communicate, which would defeat the purpose of a connected network. Think of it like different neighborhoods in a city; they are distinct, but they need roads and bridges to connect them. Inter-VLAN routing provides those vital connections.

keyIdea.title: Bridging Subnets
keyIdea.text: VLANs create separate IP subnets, requiring a Layer 3 device to route traffic between them for communication.

screens.title: Layer 3 Switches and Switched Virtual Interfaces (SVIs)
screens.subtitle: Enabling Routing Capabilities on a Switch

narration.text: Now that we understand the problem, let's explore the solution: Layer 3 switches and Switched Virtual Interfaces, or SVIs. Modern Arista switches are often capable of performing Layer 3 routing in addition to their primary Layer 2 switching functions. When a switch has this capability, we refer to it as a Layer 3 switch. This means it can not only forward frames within the same VLAN but also route packets between different IP subnets, effectively acting like a router. The key component that enables a Layer 3 switch to route between VLANs is the Switched Virtual Interface, or SVI. You might also hear it called a VLAN interface. An SVI is a logical Layer 3 interface that you associate with a specific VLAN. It's not a physical port, but a virtual one that exists within the switch's software. Crucially, an SVI acts as the default gateway for all devices within its associated VLAN. For example, if you have VLAN 10, its SVI will have an IP address like 192.168.10.1, which devices in VLAN 10 will use as their gateway to reach other networks. This allows the Layer 3 switch to intercept traffic destined for other VLANs and route it accordingly. Understanding the SVI's role as the gateway is fundamental to configuring inter-VLAN routing successfully.

keyIdea.title: SVI as Gateway
keyIdea.text: A Layer 3 switch uses SVIs as logical Layer 3 interfaces, acting as default gateways for VLANs to enable inter-VLAN routing.

screens.title: How SVIs Facilitate Inter-VLAN Communication
screens.subtitle: Understanding the Routing Process on a Layer 3 Switch

narration.text: Let's delve deeper into how SVIs actually facilitate inter-VLAN communication. Imagine a device in VLAN 10, with an IP address like 192.168.10.10, wants to communicate with a device in VLAN 20, at 192.168.20.20. Since these devices are in different IP subnets, the VLAN 10 device knows it needs to send the packet to its default gateway. This default gateway, as we just discussed, is the SVI for VLAN 10, which has an IP address like 192.168.10.1. The Layer 3 switch receives this packet on the VLAN 10 SVI. Once the packet arrives at the SVI, the switch, now acting at Layer 3, examines the packet's destination IP address. It then consults its routing table to determine the best path to reach the 192.168.20.0/24 network. Assuming the routing table has an entry for VLAN 20's network, the switch will then forward the packet out the VLAN 20 SVI, which is the gateway for the destination network. The packet is then delivered to the target device in VLAN 20. This entire process happens seamlessly and quickly within the Layer 3 switch, making inter-VLAN communication transparent to the end devices. It's a fundamental mechanism for connecting your segmented network efficiently.

keyIdea.title: Routing Table Lookup
keyIdea.text: The Layer 3 switch uses its routing table to forward packets received on one SVI to the appropriate destination SVI for another VLAN.

content.html:

Packet Flow

How SVIs Facilitate Inter-VLAN Communication

The Layer 3 switch routes packets between SVIs by consulting its routing table, enabling seamless communication across VLANs.

Packet to Gateway

A device sends a packet to its default gateway (the SVI for its VLAN) when the destination is in another subnet.

Routing Table Lookup

The Layer 3 switch receives the packet on the SVI and consults its routing table for the destination network.

Forwarding to Destination

The switch forwards the packet out the SVI corresponding to the destination VLAN's network.

screens.title: Configuring SVIs on Arista EOS: An Overview
screens.subtitle: Essential Steps for Enabling Inter-VLAN Routing

narration.text: Now that we understand the 'why' and 'how' of SVIs, let's move into the practical steps of configuring them on an Arista EOS switch. Configuring SVIs involves a few critical stages that you must follow in sequence to ensure proper functionality. First and foremost, you need to ensure that the VLANs themselves are already created and properly assigned to the appropriate access or trunk ports on your switch. This is a foundational Layer 2 step that must be in place before you can configure any Layer 3 interfaces for those VLANs. Once your VLANs are defined, the next step is to create the SVI for each VLAN. This involves entering a specific configuration mode for the virtual interface. After creating the SVI, you will assign an IP address and subnet mask to it. This IP address is crucial because it will serve as the default gateway for all devices within that VLAN. It's vital that this IP address falls within the IP subnet of its corresponding VLAN. Finally, and this is a step often overlooked, you must enable global IP routing on the switch. Without this command, the switch will only perform Layer 2 forwarding, and your inter-VLAN routing will simply not function. We'll break down each of these steps with specific commands in the upcoming screens.

keyIdea.title: Sequential Configuration
keyIdea.text: SVI configuration requires creating VLANs, defining SVIs with IP addresses, and enabling global IP routing on the switch.

screens.title: VLAN Creation and Global IP Routing
screens.subtitle: The Foundational Commands for Inter-VLAN Routing

narration.text: Let's dive into the first crucial steps for configuring SVIs: creating your VLANs and enabling global IP routing. Before you can even think about assigning IP addresses to virtual interfaces, you must ensure the VLANs themselves exist on your Arista switch. This is done using the vlan command in global configuration mode, followed by an optional name command to give it a descriptive label. For example, vlan 10 and name Sales clearly defines your sales VLAN. After creating your VLANs, the next critical step is to enable global IP routing on the switch. This is achieved with the simple yet powerful ip routing command. Without this command, your Layer 3 switch will only perform Layer 2 forwarding, and any SVIs you configure will not route traffic between different VLANs. It's like having a car with an engine but no fuel; it has the capability, but it won't move. If you're working with IPv6, you'll also need to use ipv6 unicast-routing. Always remember to save your configuration after making changes. These two steps lay the groundwork for all subsequent inter-VLAN routing configurations.

keyIdea.title: Routing Foundation
keyIdea.text: VLANs must be created and global IP routing enabled before SVIs can function as Layer 3 interfaces.

content.html:
Module 4›Chapter 4.4›VLAN Creation and Global IP Routing
Step-by-Step Configuration

VLAN Creation and Global IP Routing

Establish VLANs and enable Layer 3 routing globally on the switch as the first steps for SVI functionality.

1. Create VLANs

Use vlan <VLAN_ID> and name <VLAN_Name> to define your logical network segments.

2. Enable Global IP Routing

Execute ip routing (and ipv6 unicast-routing if needed) in global config mode to activate Layer 3 forwarding.

Common Mistake

Forgetting ip routing is a frequent error that prevents inter-VLAN communication, as the switch remains a Layer 2 device.

Arista EOS Configuration Example
Arista# configure terminal
Arista(config)# vlan 10
Arista(config-vlan-10)# name Sales
Arista(config-vlan-10)# exit
Arista(config)# vlan 20
Arista(config-vlan-20)# name Marketing
Arista(config-vlan-20)# exit

Arista(config)# ip routing  # Enable global IP routing for IPv4
Arista(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing # Enable global IP routing for IPv6 (if needed)
Pro Tip

Always verify VLAN creation with show vlan before proceeding to SVI configuration.

screens.title: Configuring Switched Virtual Interfaces (SVIs)
screens.subtitle: Assigning IP Addresses to VLANs for Routing

narration.text: With VLANs created and global IP routing enabled, the next step is to configure the Switched Virtual Interfaces themselves. This is where you assign the Layer 3 identity to your VLANs. You begin by entering the SVI interface configuration mode using the command interface Vlan. For example, interface Vlan 10 will take you into the configuration context for VLAN 10's virtual interface. Once inside this mode, you assign an IP address and subnet mask to the SVI using the ip address slash command. This IP address is critically important because it will serve as the default gateway for all devices within that specific VLAN. It's imperative that the IP address you assign to the SVI falls within the IP subnet of its corresponding VLAN. For instance, if VLAN 10 is on the 192.168.10.0/24 network, its SVI should be something like 192.168.10.1/24. Finally, ensure the SVI is administratively up by using the no shutdown command. Just like physical interfaces, SVIs can be shut down, preventing them from passing traffic. This step ensures your SVI is active and ready to route. These commands are the heart of SVI configuration.

keyIdea.title: SVI IP Assignment
keyIdea.text: SVIs are configured with an IP address and subnet mask, acting as the default gateway for their respective VLANs.

content.html:
Module 4›Chapter 4.4›Configuring SVIs
Step-by-Step Configuration

Configuring Switched Virtual Interfaces (SVIs)

Define logical Layer 3 interfaces for each VLAN by assigning IP addresses and ensuring they are active.

1. Enter SVI Interface Mode

Use interface Vlan <VLAN_ID> to configure the specific virtual interface.

2. Assign IP Address

Set the SVI's IP address and subnet mask (e.g., ip address 192.168.10.1/24).

3. Activate SVI

Ensure the SVI is administratively up with the no shutdown command.

Common Mistake

Assigning an SVI IP address outside its VLAN's subnet will cause routing failures for that VLAN.

Arista EOS Configuration Example
Arista(config)# interface Vlan 10
Arista(config-if-Vl10)# description Sales_VLAN_SVI
Arista(config-if-Vl10)# ip address 192.168.10.1/24
Arista(config-if-Vl10)# no shutdown
Arista(config-if-Vl10)# exit

Arista(config)# interface Vlan 20
Arista(config-if-Vl20)# description Marketing_VLAN_SVI
Arista(config-if-Vl20)# ip address 192.168.20.1/24
Arista(config-if-Vl20)# no shutdown
Arista(config-if-Vl20)# exit
Pro Tip

Use descriptive descriptions for your SVIs to easily identify their purpose.

screens.title: Assigning Physical Ports to VLANs
screens.subtitle: Connecting End Devices to Your Segmented Network

narration.text: While configuring SVIs is crucial for Layer 3 routing, it's equally important to ensure your end devices can actually connect to these VLANs at Layer 2. This involves assigning physical switch ports to their respective VLANs. Without this step, even with perfectly configured SVIs, your devices won't be able to reach their default gateways. For example, to connect a device to VLAN 10, you would enter the interface configuration mode for a specific Ethernet port, such as interface Ethernet 1. Then, you configure the port as an access port using switchport mode access and assign it to VLAN 10 with switchport access vlan 10. Remember to use no shutdown to ensure the physical port is active. Similarly, for a device in VLAN 20, you would assign another Ethernet port, say Ethernet 2, to VLAN 20. This process ensures that when a device plugs into that physical port, its traffic is immediately associated with the correct VLAN and, consequently, can utilize the SVI as its default gateway for inter-VLAN communication. This completes the Layer 2 connectivity, allowing the Layer 3 routing to take over when traffic needs to cross VLAN boundaries. It's the bridge between your physical network and your logical VLAN segmentation.

keyIdea.title: Layer 2 Connectivity
keyIdea.text: Physical ports must be assigned to VLANs as access ports to connect end devices and enable them to use SVIs as gateways.

content.html:
Module 4›Chapter 4.4›Assigning Physical Ports to VLANs
Practical Application

Assigning Physical Ports to VLANs

Connect end devices to your VLANs by configuring physical switch ports as access ports and assigning them to the correct VLAN ID.

1. Enter Interface Mode

Navigate to the specific physical Ethernet interface (e.g., interface Ethernet 1).

2. Configure as Access Port

Set the port mode to access: switchport mode access.

3. Assign to VLAN

Assign the port to its respective VLAN: switchport access vlan <VLAN_ID>.

4. Activate Port

Ensure the port is active with no shutdown.

Arista EOS Configuration Example
Arista(config)# interface Ethernet 1
Arista(config-if-Et1)# description Sales_Access_Port
Arista(config-if-Et1)# switchport mode access
Arista(config-if-Et1)# switchport access vlan 10
Arista(config-if-Et1)# no shutdown
Arista(config-if-Et1)# exit

Arista(config)# interface Ethernet 2
Arista(config-if-Et2)# description Marketing_Access_Port
Arista(config-if-Et2)# switchport mode access
Arista(config-if-Et2)# switchport access vlan 20
Arista(config-if-Et2)# no shutdown
Arista(config-if-Et2)# exit
Pro Tip

Always use descriptive descriptions for your physical interfaces to aid in network documentation and troubleshooting.

narration.text: After you've meticulously configured your SVIs and assigned your physical ports, verification is absolutely critical. You need to confirm that everything is working as expected and that inter-VLAN routing is operational. There are several key show commands you can use on an Arista EOS switch. First, show ip interface brief Vlan is essential. This command will display the IP address, subnet mask, and operational status of your SVI. You should see the SVI listed with its correct IP address and a status of 'up/up', indicating it's administratively and operationally active. If it's 'down/down', you might have forgotten the no shutdown command or there's an underlying VLAN issue. Next, show ip route connected is vital. This command will show you all directly connected networks, which should include the networks associated with your SVIs. Seeing these routes confirms that the switch recognizes the VLAN subnets as directly reachable via their respective SVIs. Finally, the ultimate test is to ping from the switch to devices in different VLANs, or even better, from a device in one VLAN to a device in another VLAN, using its SVI as the gateway. Successful pings confirm end-to-end Layer 3 connectivity. These verification steps are your safety net, ensuring your network changes have the desired effect.

keyIdea.title: Confirming Connectivity
keyIdea.text: Use `show` commands and `ping` to verify SVI status, routing table entries, and inter-VLAN connectivity.

content.html:
Module 4›Chapter 4.4›Verifying SVI Configurations
Verification

Verifying SVI Configurations

Confirm SVI operational status, IP address assignment, routing table entries, and end-to-end connectivity.

1. Check SVI Status

Use show ip interface brief Vlan <VLAN_ID> to confirm IP and 'up/up' status.

2. Verify Connected Routes

Run show ip route connected to ensure VLAN networks are recognized as directly connected.

3. Test Connectivity

Use ping from the switch or end devices to confirm inter-VLAN communication.

Arista EOS Verification Commands
Arista# show ip interface brief Vlan 10
Arista# show ip interface brief Vlan 20
Arista# show ip route connected
Arista# ping 192.168.20.1 # Ping SVI in another VLAN
Arista# ping 192.168.20.10 # Ping host in another VLAN
Pro Tip

Always test connectivity from both the switch and actual end devices to ensure full network reachability.

screens.title: Common Inter-VLAN Routing Issues
screens.subtitle: Diagnosing and Resolving SVI Configuration Problems

narration.text: Even with careful configuration, you might encounter issues with inter-VLAN routing. Knowing how to troubleshoot these common problems is a vital skill. One of the most frequent mistakes is forgetting to enable global IP routing using the ip routing command. If this command is missing, your Layer 3 switch will simply not route, and packets will remain isolated within their VLANs. Another common issue is assigning an incorrect IP address to the SVI. Remember, the SVI's IP address must fall within the IP subnet of its corresponding VLAN. If it doesn't, devices in that VLAN won't be able to reach their default gateway, leading to communication failures. A third common problem is failing to assign physical ports to the respective VLANs. If an end device is plugged into a port that isn't correctly configured for its VLAN, it won't be able to communicate with anything, including its SVI. Lastly, always check if an SVI is administratively shut down. If you forget the no shutdown command, the SVI will be inactive. Always approach troubleshooting systematically: check global routing, then SVI IP addresses and status, and finally, physical port assignments. Misconfigurations can lead to complete loss of connectivity, so always test changes in a controlled environment first.

keyIdea.title: Systematic Diagnosis
keyIdea.text: Troubleshoot inter-VLAN routing by checking global IP routing, SVI IP addresses, SVI status, and physical port assignments.

Module 4›Chapter 4.4›Common Inter-VLAN Routing Issues
Troubleshooting

Common Inter-VLAN Routing Issues

Identify and resolve frequent configuration errors that prevent inter-VLAN communication on Arista EOS switches.

Missing ip routing

The switch will not perform Layer 3 routing without this global command.

Incorrect SVI IP Address

SVI IP must match the VLAN's subnet; otherwise, devices cannot reach their gateway.

Physical Port Assignment

Ensure physical access ports are correctly assigned to their respective VLANs.

Shutdown SVI

An SVI must have no shutdown applied to be administratively up and active.

Troubleshooting Flow
Is ip routing enabled?
Are SVI IPs correct & 'up/up'?
Are physical ports assigned?
Connectivity Restored!
Key Takeaway

Systematic troubleshooting, starting from global routing and moving to interface-specific configurations, is key to resolving inter-VLAN routing issues.

narration.text: As we conclude this chapter, let's recap the key concepts that are fundamental to understanding inter-VLAN routing. First, Inter-VLAN Routing itself is the process of forwarding network traffic between different Virtual Local Area Networks. It's the mechanism that allows your segmented VLANs to communicate, transforming isolated islands into a connected network. Next, we have the Layer 3 Switch. This is a powerful network device that can perform both Layer 2 switching and Layer 3 routing functions. It's the hardware foundation that enables inter-VLAN routing without needing a separate physical router. Finally, the Switched Virtual Interface, or SVI, is a logical Layer 3 interface on a Layer 3 switch. It's associated with a specific VLAN and, crucially, acts as the default gateway for all devices within that VLAN. Think of it as the virtual bridge connecting your VLAN to the routing capabilities of the Layer 3 switch. These three concepts form the core of inter-VLAN routing, allowing for efficient and scalable network designs.

keyIdea.title: Routing Fundamentals
keyIdea.text: Inter-VLAN routing, Layer 3 switches, and SVIs are the core components for connecting segmented networks.

Key Concepts: Inter-VLAN Routing

Review the foundational terms and ideas from this chapter.

Inter-VLAN Routing

The process of forwarding network traffic between different Virtual Local Area Networks (VLANs).

Layer 3 Switch

A switch that can perform both Layer 2 switching and Layer 3 routing functions.

Switched Virtual Interface (SVI)

A logical Layer 3 interface on a Layer 3 switch associated with a specific VLAN, acting as its default gateway.

Chapter Summary

Inter-VLAN routing is essential for connecting segmented VLANs. Layer 3 switches, utilizing SVIs, provide the necessary routing capabilities by acting as default gateways for each VLAN, enabling seamless communication across different IP subnets.

narration.text: Let's continue our review of key concepts, focusing on broader routing essentials. First, the Default Gateway is a critical concept. It's the IP address of the router or Layer 3 switch that devices in a subnet use to send traffic to destinations outside their local subnet. Without a correctly configured default gateway, a device cannot communicate beyond its immediate VLAN. It's the exit ramp from your local network segment. Second, we have the ip routing command. This is a global configuration command on Arista EOS and other network devices that explicitly enables the device to perform Layer 3 routing. It's a fundamental command that transforms a Layer 2 switch into a Layer 3 routing device. Forgetting this command is a common pitfall that prevents inter-VLAN communication. Together, these concepts ensure that your network devices can not only communicate within their local segments but also reach resources and devices across different VLANs and even out to the wider internet. Mastering these terms is key to building and managing complex network infrastructures effectively.

keyIdea.title: Routing Enablement
keyIdea.text: The default gateway and the `ip routing` command are crucial for enabling devices to communicate beyond their local subnet.

Key Concepts: Routing Essentials

Reinforce your understanding of fundamental routing components.

Default Gateway

The IP address of the router or Layer 3 switch that devices use to send traffic outside their local subnet.

ip routing Command

A global configuration command that enables a network device to perform Layer 3 routing functions.

Network Segmentation

Dividing a network into smaller, isolated logical segments (VLANs) for security, performance, and management.

Chapter Summary

The default gateway is the exit point for local subnet traffic, and the ip routing command activates Layer 3 forwarding. These are crucial for enabling communication across segmented networks.
